Finds and excavations · Archaeology · Linguistics and scripts

Faded red inscriptions reported in a rock shelter at Manchirevula, on the edge of Hyderabad

Heritage volunteers say traces of painted letters on a boulder wall near the Manchirevula Forest Trek Park range from Brahmi of about the 1st century to Telugu-Kannada script of about the 7th century.

Talaash Heritage desk · Published 26 November 2026

Where
Manchirevula, near Hyderabad, Telangana

Members of the Kotha Telangana Charitra Brundam, a Telangana heritage research group, together with the groups Save Rocks and Climate Front Telangana, have reported red-coloured inscriptions on the face of a boulder under a rock overhang near Hyderabad. It lies on a hill beside the one crowned by the Ghar-e-Mubarak Dargah, near the Manchirevula Forest Trek Park. Siasat and Telangana Today reported the find on 21 November 2026 and Deccan Chronicle on 22 November.

According to the reports, the site had earlier yielded rock art and Palaeolithic tools. Kavali Chandrakanth of the Brundam located the inscribed surface, and the team that inspected it included the group's president, Sriramoju Haragopal, Mir Omar Ali Khan of Climate Front Telangana, Sudhir Bhanu of Save Rocks, and Siddhartha. The team says the red marks are writing, not paintings.

Haragopal's reading, as reported, finds traces of five inscriptions, with surviving characters including 'Vi', 'Ta', 'Tarah', '(Ku)shta Charu' and 'Duru'. He assigns the surviving letters to two scripts: Brahmi of about the 1st century CE and the Telugu-Kannada script of about the 7th century; Siasat reports 'Vi' as Brahmi and 'Duru' as Telugu-Kannada. Deccan Chronicle reports that rain has stripped away most of the red colour, leaving the writing hard to make out.

The Brundam has previously recorded label inscriptions and isolated letters beside rock paintings at other rock-art sites, among them Pandavulagutta, Wargal and Seethammaloddi. Haragopal, as quoted by Telangana Today, said that the presence of actual inscriptions, not only paintings, is what makes the site significant.

The dates and readings so far come from the research group, as reported in the press. The reports do not say whether the state archaeology department or the Archaeological Survey of India has examined the shelter, and none gives a full transcript of the writing. The researchers say the site needs proper documentation, protection and further study before the meaning of the writing can be settled.
